inputs.need:
I am an epidemiologist in the tobacco control unit of the Carrow State Health Department. Our state introduced tobacco retail licensing in 2019, so we now have a geocoded list of every licensed retailer, about 2,300 of them, and several local councils want to cap the number of licences near schools. Before the state backs those caps, the minister's office has asked whether students at schools with more tobacco retailers nearby are more likely to smoke or vape.

I would like to run a cross-sectional analysis that links the number of licensed retailers within 800 metres of each secondary school to students' current smoking and current vaping in the 2025 school health survey, adjusting for school socioeconomic status and remoteness. I know this cannot show that retailer density causes smoking, and I want the design to be honest about that. I also want to check whether the association differs for vaping, because many licensed retailers now sell vapes, and whether it holds in regional towns as well as the capital.

What I need: a clear question, the right unit of analysis (students within schools), which confounders matter, how to handle schools with no retailer nearby, and a sense of what the published evidence shows. The survey is held by a separate custodian, and student data can only be analysed through the custodian's secure analysis service, which we have not yet applied to.
inputs.constraints: Secondary data only: the licence list and the 2025 school health survey. One analyst for four months from January 2027. School and student identities stay with the survey custodian; analysis only through the custodian's secure analysis service.
localFacts: The state licence list held 2,312 active tobacco retail licences on 2026-07-01, each with a geocoded address.
The 2025 school health survey sampled 186 secondary schools and about 24,400 students in grades 8 to 12.
No application has yet been made to the survey custodian's secure analysis service, which accepts applications monthly.

records.title: Tobacco retailer density within 800 metres of schools and current smoking among secondary students: a multilevel cross-sectional study
records.authors: Achterberg-Lowe P, Nyambura-Hayes C, Ivanova-Price M
records.abstract: We linked a 2017 school survey of 31,200 students in 212 secondary schools to a state list of licensed tobacco retailers. Students at schools with five or more retailers within 800 metres had higher odds of current smoking than students at schools with none (odds ratio 1.31, 95 percent CI 1.08 to 1.59) after adjustment for school socioeconomic status, remoteness and student age and sex. There was no clear dose-response between one and four retailers. The association was similar in metropolitan and regional schools. Cross-sectional data cannot establish whether retailers locate near schools with more demand.

records.title: Retailer density near schools and student vaping: evidence from two survey waves
records.abstract: Using two waves of a school health survey (2021 and 2023) linked to licensed retailer locations, we examined current vaping among 18,700 students. In 2023, students at schools with three or more retailers within 800 metres had higher odds of current vaping (odds ratio 1.22, 95 percent CI 1.03 to 1.45); in 2021 the association was weaker and its interval included 1. Adjustment for school socioeconomic status reduced both associations by about a third. Vape-only retailers were not licensed in the study period and could not be counted.

records.title: Outlet density and youth smoking after adjustment for area deprivation: a cross-sectional study in three cities
records.abstract: In three cities, we related the density of tobacco outlets around 96 secondary schools to current smoking among 14,900 students. The unadjusted association was strong (odds ratio 1.62 for the highest against the lowest density quartile), but after adjustment for neighbourhood deprivation it fell to 1.09 (95 percent CI 0.88 to 1.35). Deprivation was associated with both outlet density and smoking. The authors caution that density limits may do less than expected if deprivation drives both, and recommend analyses that model deprivation carefully.

records.title: Buffer size and exposure measurement for retail environment studies around schools
records.abstract: We compared retailer counts within 400, 800 and 1,600 metres of 150 schools, using road network distance and straight-line distance. Counts within 800 metres by road network distance best reflected the routes students reported walking between school and home or shops. Straight-line buffers overstated exposure for schools near rivers, rail lines and highways. Associations with student smoking were strongest for the 800 metre road network buffer. About one school in five had no retailer within 800 metres, which should be modelled as a separate category rather than as a low count.

records.title: Where students buy cigarettes and vapes: purchase locations reported in a state school survey
records.abstract: Among 2,640 students who reported current smoking or vaping in a state school survey, 36 percent of smokers and 44 percent of vapers said they had bought their own product in the past month, mostly from convenience stores and service stations. Students aged under 16 were less likely to report buying their own product and more likely to obtain it from friends or siblings. Purchasing near school was reported by 18 percent of those who bought their own. The survey did not verify purchase locations.

records.title: Licensing caps on tobacco outlets near schools: an evaluation five years after introduction
records.authors: Morrow-Adebayo J, Linde-Chukwu O, Pereira-Vance S
records.abstract: A state capped new tobacco licences within 500 metres of schools in 2019. Five years later the number of licensed outlets within 500 metres of schools had fallen by 23 percent, mostly through closures rather than refusals. Current smoking among students fell in both capped and comparison areas, and the difference in the decline between areas was small and imprecise (1.4 percentage points, 95 percent CI -0.9 to 3.7). The evaluation could not separate the cap from other tobacco control measures introduced in the same period.

records.title: Measuring current smoking and vaping in school surveys: agreement with saliva cotinine
records.abstract: School surveys rely on students' own reports of smoking and vaping. In a validation sub-study of 1,120 students from 40 schools, self-reported current smoking agreed well with saliva cotinine (sensitivity 0.87, specificity 0.96), but self-reported vaping could not be validated because cotinine does not separate nicotine sources. Reporting was more accurate when surveys were completed without teachers present and when students were told that answers could not be traced to them. The authors recommend defining current use as any use in the past 30 days and reporting smoking and vaping separately.

response.synthesis: Seven retrieved records, appraised at abstract level. Two cross-sectional studies found higher odds of smoking or vaping with more retailers near schools after adjustment for school socioeconomic status, but a three-city study found the smoking association largely explained by neighbourhood deprivation, so the evidence conflicts on confounding. An 800 metre road network buffer is the best-supported exposure, with no-retailer schools as their own category. The only evaluation of a cap found fewer outlets but no clear change in smoking. None of this shows that density causes smoking.
response.gradeRationale: Cross-sectional studies with inconsistent results after deprivation adjustment and one non-randomised policy evaluation; indirect for a causal policy question.
response.summary: Seven retrieved records appraised; four claims recorded, two of them in conflict; overall certainty low.

response.reading: Retailer density, deprivation and student smoking form a triangle: deprived neighbourhoods have more retailers and more smoking, so the density association can be real, confounded or both. The retrieved studies disagree precisely on this point. Purchasing near school explains only part of access, and vaping may follow a different pattern from smoking because vapes are sold through different outlets.

response.designSummary: Multilevel logistic regression with students nested in schools; exposure at school level in three categories.
response.sampleSize: The sample is fixed by the survey: about 24,400 students in 186 schools, a mean of about 131 per school. With an intraclass correlation near 0.03 for smoking, the design effect is about 1 + 130 x 0.03 = 4.9, giving an effective sample near 5,000. If about 15 percent of students attend schools with five or more retailers and current smoking is near 6 percent, this is enough to estimate an odds ratio of 1.3 with a 95 percent interval roughly from 1.05 to 1.6; smaller associations will be imprecise. About one school in five is expected in the no-retailer reference group.
response.primaryAnalysis: Odds ratios for 1 to 4 and 5 or more retailers against none, with 95 percent confidence intervals, adjusted for school socioeconomic index, neighbourhood deprivation, remoteness, age and sex; random intercept for school.
response.secondaryAnalysis: Same model for current vaping; estimates by remoteness (capital, regional); sensitivity analysis with a 400 metre buffer.
response.missingData: Students missing the outcome are excluded and counted; schools that cannot be geocoded are listed and compared with linked schools.

Our state introduced tobacco retail licensing in 2019, so we now have a geocoded list of every licensed retailer, about 2,300 of them, and several local councils want to cap the number of licences near schools. I would like to run a cross-sectional analysis that links the number of licensed retailers within 800 metres of each secondary school to students' current smoking and current vaping in the 2025 school health survey, adjusting for school socioeconomic status and remoteness. I know this cannot show that retailer density causes smoking, and I want the design to be honest about that. I also want to check whether the association differs for vaping, because many licensed retailers now sell vapes, and whether it holds in regional towns as well as the capital.

What I need: a clear question, the right unit of analysis (students within schools), which confounders matter, how to handle schools with no retailer nearby, and a sense of what the published evidence shows. The survey is held by a separate custodian, and student data can only be analysed through the custodian's secure analysis service, which we have not yet applied to.
